raw_case_text:
A 6-month-old boy with hydrocephalus was referred to our hospital in 2008. The hydrocephalus during the first admission was confirmed by computed tomography (CT) scan. Examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) did not reveal any abnormality.
A VP shunt was inserted in June 2008 and the infant was discharged in acceptable condition, with good control of hydrocephalus confirmed by another CT scan on discharge day. Approximately 16 months after insertion of the VP shunt, the child was readmitted with a one-week history of fever (up to 38.5 C), and acute abdominal pain. The diagnosis was brucellosis based on serum agglutination test 1/640 and 1/1280 three days later. A titre of 1/320 measured in 2 mercaptoethanol (2ME) test. The patient was treated with trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole, rifampin, and gentamicin. His blood culture was negative.
The Ascitic fluid examination showed a glucose level of 89 mg/dL, a protein level of 5800 mg/dL, white blood cell (WBC) count was 480 (10% polymorphonuclear cells and 90% mononuclear), and the red blood cell (RBC) count was 4800.
After 4 months, he was again admitted to our hospital with drowsiness, vomiting and fever. Clinical diagnosis was suggestive for a VP shunt infection. Laboratory results were as follows: Hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL; WBC count, 6.1x103 cells/mm3. 
A sample of ventricular CSF analyzed was slightly xanthochromic and contained a total of 4000 cells (70% polymorphonuclear cells and 30% lymphocytes), 80 mg/ dL glucose, and 192 mg/dL protein. No organisms were observed on the direct gram-stained smear. 
Blood culture was sterile and CSF serological test was positive (Brucella agglutinin titer was 1/80).
The patient responded well to a course of rifampin, gentamicin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily. Three days later the shunt was extracted. He was well on three follow-up visits at the outpatient clinic and the latest follow-up visit was 12 months after the diagnosis has been made. Figure 1 and 2 show Brain CT scan before and after extracting the VP shunt, respectively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-month-old boy with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt placed at 6 months of age presented with a 1-week history of fever up to 38.5 C and acute abdominal pain, followed 4 months later by drowsiness, vomiting, and recurrent fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A male infant who underwent ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt insertion at 6 months of age (June 2008) for hydrocephalus presented 16 months later with 1 week of fever (38.5 C) and acute abdominal pain (peritonitis/ascites), treated medically for brucellosis without shunt removal. Four months after that episode, he was readmitted with drowsiness, vomiting, and fever suggestive of ascending VP shunt neurobrucellosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Congenital/infantile hydrocephalus diagnosed at 6 months of age and treated with VP shunt insertion in June 2008; brucellous peritonitis 16 months post-shunt insertion.
subjective.review_of_systems: First readmission: Positive for fever (38.5 C) and acute abdominal pain. Second readmission (4 months later): Positive for drowsiness, vomiting, and fever.

objective.physical_examination: First readmission: febrile up to 38.5 C with acute abdominal pain/ascites. Second readmission (4 months later): drowsy and febrile with clinical signs of VP shunt infection.
objective.routine_investigations: Second readmission CBC: hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, WBC 6.1 x 10^3/mm3. Blood cultures at both readmissions were sterile.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline and post-shunt brain CT scans confirmed hydrocephalus and shunt position. First readmission ascitic fluid analysis: WBC 480/mm3 (90% mononuclear, 10% polymorphonuclear), RBC 4,800/mm3, protein 5,800 mg/dL, glucose 89 mg/dL. Second readmission ventricular CSF analysis: slightly xanthochromic fluid with WBC 4,000/mm3 (70% polymorphonuclear, 30% lymphocytes), protein 192 mg/dL, glucose 80 mg/dL, and negative Gram stain.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: At the first readmission, serum Brucella agglutination titer was 1:640 rising to 1:1,280 three days later (2-mercaptoethanol titer 1:320), and at the second readmission ventricular CSF Brucella agglutination titer was positive at 1:80, confirming Brucella ventriculoperitoneal shunt infection presenting initially with peritonitis/ascites and subsequently with ventriculitis. Medical therapy alone at the first readmission (TMP-SMX, rifampin, and gentamicin) was followed by relapse 4 months later; definitive cure was achieved at the second admission by combining daily rifampin, gentamicin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with complete VP shunt extraction on day 3, with the child remaining healthy at 12-month follow-up.
